title: Tiredness and Fever - Infective Endocarditis on Rheumatic Heart Disease
patient_instructions: You are Daniel Foster, a 46-year-old man. For about three weeks you have felt increasingly tired, run-down and hot/feverish, with body aches. You have not actually measured your temperature. You are worried because it is not going away. Key story (reveal when asked): as a child you were told you had a 'heart murmur' and you took antibiotics for a long time when you were young, but you stopped in your teens and have had no heart follow-up since. About three weeks ago you had a root canal at the dentist - you were not given any antibiotics before it. You have NOT injected drugs. You have no significant shortness of breath, no chest pain, no leg swelling, and no recent sore throats. No night sweats or weight loss that you have noticed. You have no other medical problems and take no regular medications. If asked about ethnicity/background, you can answer as directed by the examiner. Your concern, if asked: 'Why can't I shake this off? Is it something serious with my heart?' Affect: tired, a bit worried, cooperative. Only volunteer the childhood murmur and the recent dental work if the candidate asks relevant questions.
candidate_instructions: You are the GP. Daniel Foster, 46, presents with three weeks of tiredness and feeling feverish. Your tasks: (1) Take a focused history. (2) You may ask the examiner for physical examination findings (PEFE). (3) Explain your most likely diagnosis and reasoning to the patient. (4) Outline your immediate investigation and management plan. You have 8 minutes.
examiner_instructions: This station tests recognition of infective endocarditis as a serious not-to-miss cause of subacute fever and fatigue, and its emergency management. Reward the candidate for exploring the tiredness and fever, then taking a targeted cardiac/endocarditis history: childhood murmur, prolonged childhood antibiotics with no follow-up (rheumatic fever / rheumatic heart disease and lapsed secondary prophylaxis), recent root canal WITHOUT antibiotic prophylaxis, and no IV drug use. On PEFE, provide when asked: febrile; no cachexia or rashes; no lymphadenopathy; normal thyroid; on auscultation S1 and S2 normal with a mid-diastolic rumbling murmur best at the mitral area (mitral stenosis); splinter haemorrhages present; no Osler nodes or Janeway lesions; urine dipstick may show microscopic haematuria. The candidate must state infective endocarditis, recognise it as a life-threatening emergency, and escalate: urgent hospital/ED referral for at least 3 sets of blood cultures from separate sites BEFORE antibiotics, transthoracic (and possibly transoesophageal) echocardiography, empirical IV antibiotics per eTG, and application of the modified Duke criteria. Reward mention of the preventable link (missed antibiotic prophylaxis before dental work in RHD) and the ARF/RHD register/secondary prophylaxis, plus the raised ARF/RHD prevalence in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. Prompt if needed: 'How urgently does this need to be actioned?'

criteria: Explores tiredness and fever: duration (~3 weeks), meaning, associated malaise, and effect on daily life
Takes a targeted cardiac history: childhood murmur, prolonged childhood antibiotics, no follow-up (rheumatic heart disease with lapsed prophylaxis)
Identifies the endocarditis trigger: recent root canal without antibiotic prophylaxis; asks about IV drug use
Screens differentials: cardiac failure symptoms, other infections (pneumonia, UTI), and malignancy (weight loss, night sweats)
Requests a focused CVS examination and correctly interprets the mid-diastolic rumbling mitral murmur as mitral stenosis (rheumatic)
Elicits and recognises peripheral stigmata (splinter haemorrhages, microscopic haematuria) as Duke minor criteria
States infective endocarditis as the diagnosis and explains the pathophysiology chain (RHD-damaged valve + bacteraemia from dental work)
Notes that diagnosis is formalised with the modified Duke criteria
Recognises infective endocarditis as a life-threatening emergency requiring urgent hospital/ED referral
Arranges at least 3 sets of blood cultures from separate sites BEFORE starting antibiotics
Requests echocardiography (transthoracic and often transoesophageal) plus FBE, CRP/ESR, urinalysis and ECG
Starts empirical IV antibiotics per Therapeutic Guidelines once cultures are taken
Highlights prevention: antibiotic prophylaxis before dental/invasive procedures in RHD, ARF/RHD register and secondary prophylaxis (benzathine penicillin)
Explains the diagnosis and its seriousness in clear, plain language and addresses the patient's concern
Communicates the urgency and the plan calmly, and notes the higher ARF/RHD burden in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities where relevant

red_flags: Prolonged fever with fatigue plus a new/changing murmur - infective endocarditis, a life-threatening emergency
Peripheral stigmata: splinter haemorrhages, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots and microscopic haematuria (immune-complex glomerulonephritis) as Duke minor criteria
Rheumatic heart disease with a dental procedure and no antibiotic prophylaxis - the key preventable link
Risk of valve destruction, embolic stroke and heart failure if antibiotics are delayed - blood cultures must precede antibiotics
australian_guidelines: Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) - suspected infective endocarditis: take at least 3 sets of blood cultures from separate sites before empirical IV antibiotics, and arrange echocardiography; diagnosis formalised with the modified Duke criteria
Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) - antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g. amoxicillin) before certain dental/invasive procedures for high-risk cardiac conditions including rheumatic heart disease

RHDAustralia / Australian ARF-RHD Guideline - secondary prophylaxis with benzathine benzylpenicillin and registration on the ARF/RHD register; markedly higher prevalence in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities
RACGP - subacute fever with fatigue and a cardiac murmur warrants urgent assessment for infective endocarditis rather than routine outpatient management
learning_objectives: Recognise infective endocarditis as a serious not-to-miss cause of subacute fever and fatigue, especially with underlying rheumatic heart disease
Link the pathophysiology chain: rheumatic fever to mitral stenosis to dental bacteraemia to endocarditis on a damaged valve
State the emergency work-up: 3 sets of blood cultures before antibiotics, echocardiography, modified Duke criteria and empirical IV antibiotics per eTG
Identify the preventable failure of antibiotic prophylaxis and the role of the ARF/RHD register and secondary prophylaxis
key_points: A new or changing murmur with fever is infective endocarditis until proven otherwise
Always take at least 3 sets of blood cultures from separate sites BEFORE giving antibiotics
Splinter haemorrhages, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots and microscopic haematuria are Duke minor criteria
Rheumatic heart disease is a high-risk condition requiring antibiotic prophylaxis before invasive dental work; the missed root-canal prophylaxis is the preventable link
ARF/RHD is far more common in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander populations - capture Indigenous status and RHD register/recall

citations.claim: Infective endocarditis appears among the serious systemic infective causes to consider in unwell patients, supporting IE as a serious not-to-miss cause of fever with tiredness.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.1949

citations.claim: Features favouring heart failure such as elevated JVP and ankle oedema (absent here) support excluding heart failure during the cardiovascular screen.
A benign viral illness is a standard comparator for a few weeks of fatigue and low-grade fever, relevant to ruling out other infections before committing to endocarditis.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.957
